title: Containers
scopeHtml: Scope: namespaces, cgroups, how Docker works, CPU throttling, OOM in containers and debugging. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: A container is a process with blinders
notes.html:
A container is not a small virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process (or group of processes) that the kernel has been told to show a limited view of the system, and to limit in resource use. There is no guest kernel: every container on a host shares the host's kernel.

Two kernel features do all the work:

  • Namespaces limit what a process can see (its own process list, network, mounts, hostname, users).
  • cgroups (control groups) limit what a process can use (CPU, memory, I/O, number of processes).
  • Plus a layered file system (overlayfs) for the image, capabilities, seccomp and LSMs (AppArmor/SELinux) for restricting what it may do.

Worked example. Start a container and look at it from the host:

$ docker run -d --name web --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 nginx
$ docker top web
UID  PID   PPID  CMD
root 18211 18190 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
$ ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -p 18211          # on the HOST it is just a process
  PID  PPID CMD
18211 18190 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
$ docker exec web ps aux | head -2     # INSIDE it thinks it is PID 1
PID USER  COMMAND
  1 root  nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;

Same process: host PID 18211, container PID 1. That one fact explains most of Docker.

VM vs container.

VM Container
Kernel Own guest kernel on virtual hardware Host kernel, shared
Start time Seconds to minutes Milliseconds to ~1 s
Overhead GB of RAM per guest MBs
Isolation Strong (hypervisor boundary) Weaker (kernel bug or misconfig can escape)
Density Tens per host Hundreds to thousands per host

Industry examples. Google ran containers on cgroups for years before Docker (Borg); Kubernetes descends from that. AWS Lambda and Fargate use Firecracker microVMs because multi-tenant strangers need VM-grade isolation. gVisor and Kata Containers add a user-space kernel or a light VM for the same reason.

Everyday analogy. Flats in one building: separate front doors and rooms (namespaces), a water and electricity meter each (cgroups), but one shared foundation (the kernel). A VM is a separate house.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying containers have their own kernel. They do not; uname -r inside equals the host's.
  • Treating containers as a security boundary equal to VMs for untrusted code.

notes.title: Namespaces
notes.html:
A namespace wraps a global system resource so that processes inside see their own private instance. Each is created with a flag to clone(), unshare() or setns().

Namespace Flag Isolates Effect
PID CLONE_NEWPID Process IDs First process is PID 1; cannot see host processes
NET CLONE_NEWNET Interfaces, routes, iptables, ports Own eth0, own port 80
MNT CLONE_NEWNS Mount points Own root file system view
UTS CLONE_NEWUTS Hostname Container name as hostname
IPC CLONE_NEWIPC SysV IPC, POSIX queues Private shared memory
USER CLONE_NEWUSER UID/GID mapping Root inside = unprivileged outside
CGROUP CLONE_NEWCGROUP cgroup root view Hides host cgroup paths
TIME CLONE_NEWTIME Boot/monotonic clock offset Rarely used 
$ sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts bash       # make your own mini-container
# hostname demo; ps aux
USER  PID COMMAND
root    1 bash
root    9 ps aux
$ ls -l /proc/18211/ns          # every process's namespace handles
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 0 net -> 'net:[4026532601]'
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 0 pid -> 'pid:[4026532599]'
$ sudo nsenter -t 18211 -n ss -ltn    # enter just its network namespace from the host
LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80

nsenter is the tool to debug a container whose image has no tools: run the host's ss, tcpdump, strace inside its namespaces.

Container networking. Docker creates a veth pair (a virtual cable): one end inside the container's net namespace as eth0, the other plugged into a bridge (docker0) on the host. NAT (iptables/nftables) sends outbound traffic out and -p 8080:80 rewrites inbound packets (DNAT). In Kubernetes, all containers of a pod share one network namespace (that is why they share localhost), and a CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, AWS VPC CNI) wires pods.

PID 1 matters. In a PID namespace the first process is init: it ignores signals it has no handler for (so docker stop's SIGTERM is ignored by a naive app, and Docker kills it after 10 s with SIGKILL), and it must reap orphaned zombies. Use docker run --init (tini) or write signal handlers.

User namespaces. Map container UID 0 to an unprivileged host UID such as 100000. Even if the process escapes, it is nobody on the host. Rootless Podman and Docker rootless use it.

Decision gravity. Running as non-root with a user namespace is cheap to adopt early and painful to retrofit when files and volumes assume UID 0. Prefer it from day one.

Industry examples. Kubernetes shares network, IPC and UTS namespaces inside a pod, but each container has its own mount and PID namespace unless shareProcessNamespace: true is set (useful for debug sidecars).

Everyday analogy. Hotel rooms: each guest has their own phone line, room numbers and bathroom (private views) but the same building.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up what namespaces do (visibility) and what cgroups do (limits).
  • Expecting a SIGTERM handler to work when the app is not PID 1 behind a shell script (CMD ./start.sh swallows signals; use exec).
  • Forgetting that the host can always see everything in the container.

notes.title: cgroups
notes.html:
Control groups account and limit resource use for a set of processes. They form a tree under /sys/fs/cgroup; each directory is a group; writing a PID into cgroup.procs moves a process in; child groups inherit and split the parent's limits. Controllers: cpu, memory, io, pids, cpuset, hugetlb, rdma.

Linux has v1 (one hierarchy per controller) and v2 (unified hierarchy, default in current distros, Docker 20.10+, Kubernetes 1.25+ GA).

$ cat /proc/18211/cgroup
0::/system.slice/docker-3f9a....scope
$ cd /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-3f9a....scope
$ cat memory.max cpu.max pids.max
536870912          # 512 MiB
150000 100000      # quota 150 ms per 100 ms period = 1.5 CPUs
max
$ cat memory.current
218103808
$ cat memory.events
low 0
high 0
max 12
oom 1
oom_kill 1         # this group has had an OOM kill

Key files (v2): memory.max (hard limit), memory.high (throttle point), memory.swap.max, cpu.max, cpu.weight (relative share, default 100), cpu.stat, io.max, pids.max, cpuset.cpus.

Two styles of limit:

  • Weights (shares): only matter under contention. cpu.weight 200 vs 100 gives 2:1 when both are busy; an idle CPU is free for anyone. Kubernetes requests map to this.
  • Hard caps: enforced always. cpu.max quota and memory.max. Kubernetes limits map to these.

Worked example (Kubernetes mapping).

resources:
  requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" }   # scheduling + cpu.weight (~ 500m -> weight)
  limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "512Mi" }   # cpu.max = 100000/100000, memory.max = 512Mi

The scheduler places the pod on a node with 500m and 256Mi free (requests). The cgroup caps it at 1 CPU and 512 MiB (limits). QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests = limits), Burstable, BestEffort (none); under node memory pressure BestEffort pods are evicted first.

Industry examples. systemd puts every service in its own cgroup (systemd-cgls, systemctl set-property nginx.service MemoryMax=1G). Google Borg, Kubernetes and Mesos all use cgroups for isolation and bin-packing.

Everyday analogy. A shared flat's utility meter with a monthly cap per tenant: the weights say who gets more when everyone is home, the hard caps say a stop-the-flow limit.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing requests are enforced limits. CPU request is a weight and scheduling hint; memory request is only used for scheduling and eviction ranking.
  • Not knowing v1 vs v2 file names (memory.limit_in_bytes vs memory.max).

notes.title: How Docker really works
notes.html:
Docker is a friendly front end over a stack of components; the Linux kernel does the real work.

  1. docker CLI sends REST calls to the dockerd daemon over /var/run/docker.sock (anyone with that socket is effectively root on the host).
  2. dockerd handles images, networks, volumes, and delegates containers to containerd (also used directly by Kubernetes via CRI).
  3. containerd manages image pulls, snapshots and container lifecycle; it starts containerd-shim per container so the container survives daemon restarts.
  4. runc (OCI reference runtime) reads the OCI bundle (config.json + root fs), calls clone with namespace flags, sets up cgroups, mounts, drops capabilities, installs seccomp, then execves your command and exits. The shim stays as the parent.

Images and layers. An image is a stack of read-only layers (tarballs of file changes, identified by SHA-256 digest) plus a config JSON. overlayfs merges them: lowerdir = read-only layers, upperdir = the container's writable layer, merged = what the process sees. Writing to a file from a lower layer triggers copy-up (copy the whole file first, then modify), so heavy writes inside the container layer are slow; use volumes.

$ docker inspect web --format '{{.GraphDriver.Data.MergedDir}}'
/var/lib/docker/overlay2/9c1a.../merged
$ mount | grep overlay
overlay on /var/lib/docker/overlay2/9c1a.../merged type overlay
  (rw,lowerdir=l/AA:l/BB:l/CC,upperdir=9c1a.../diff,workdir=9c1a.../work)
$ docker history nginx | head -4       # one layer per Dockerfile instruction

Dockerfile hygiene. Layer order controls cache reuse: put rarely changing steps (OS packages, dependency install) first and source code last. Multi-stage builds keep compilers out of the final image (Java: 700 MB build image, 150 MB runtime image).

# Dockerfile: dependency layer cached until pom.xml changes
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN mvn -B package -DskipTests
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY --from=build target/app.jar /app.jar
USER 10001
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app.jar"]

Security knobs. Default capability set is reduced (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN), default seccomp profile blocks about 40+ dangerous syscalls, --read-only root, --cap-drop ALL, --security-opt no-new-privileges. --privileged removes nearly all of it: avoid.

Volumes and state. A container's writable layer dies with it. Bind mounts and named volumes attach host directories (bypass overlayfs, good for databases).

Decision gravity. Choosing an image base (alpine/musl vs debian-slim/glibc vs distroless) is a long-lived decision: musl DNS and performance quirks, no shell for debugging in distroless (use kubectl debug ephemeral containers). Reversible via rebuild, but costs testing.

Industry examples. Kubernetes dropped dockershim (v1.24) and talks to containerd or CRI-O directly; the images stay compatible because of the OCI standards. Podman runs without a central daemon.

Everyday analogy. Docker is the shipping company's booking desk; runc is the crane that actually loads the container; the ship (kernel) carries everything.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Docker needs a hypervisor on Linux. It does not (Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows runs a hidden Linux VM).
  • Storing data in the container layer, then losing it on redeploy.
  • Running as root and mounting docker.sock into containers.

notes.title: CPU limits and throttling
notes.html:
A CPU limit in a container is a quota of CPU time per period, not a number of cores. With the CFS bandwidth controller, cpu.max = 150000 100000 means the group may use 150 ms of CPU time every 100 ms period (1.5 cores). Once the quota is spent, all threads in the group are paused until the next period, even if the machine is idle.

Limit 1 CPU = 100 ms quota per 100 ms period. App has 8 threads, all busy.
Period starts: 8 threads run in parallel on 8 cores -> 100 ms quota burns in 12.5 ms
Remaining 87.5 ms of the period: ALL threads frozen (throttled)
A request that needed 20 ms of CPU now takes 20 ms + up to 87.5 ms wait.

Symptom. Average CPU utilisation looks low (30%), yet p99 latency is bad. The cause is throttling, visible in:

$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu.stat
usage_usec 91233018221
user_usec 80112200100
system_usec 11120818121
nr_periods 612300
nr_throttled 301220          # throttled in ~49% of periods
throttled_usec 4812001299    # total throttled time ~4,812 s
$ kubectl top pod api-7d9f   # shows 300m of 1000m, looks fine!

Prometheus: rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]). Above about 5 to 25% is worth acting on.

Why multi-threaded runtimes suffer. The JVM sizes thread pools (GC threads, ForkJoin, Netty event loops) from the number of visible cores unless it detects the cgroup. Java 10+ is container aware (-XX:ActiveProcessorCount to override); Go before 1.25 saw all host cores in GOMAXPROCS (use uber-go/automaxprocs, newer Go versions respect the quota); Node and Python workers can similarly oversubscribe. A 64-core node, a 1 CPU limit, and 64 GC threads = constant throttling.

Fixes (in order).

  1. Raise or remove the CPU limit while keeping the request (many large operators, such as Tim Hockin's well-known Kubernetes advice, set CPU requests only and let pods burst; memory limit = request).
  2. Fit thread counts to the quota (GOMAXPROCS, -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2, fewer workers).
  3. Use cpuset / Kubernetes static CPU manager policy for exclusive cores (Guaranteed pods with integer CPU).
  4. Kernel burst: cpu.max.burst (cgroup v2, kernel 5.14+) lets unused quota accumulate. Older kernels had a CFS quota accounting bug fixed in 5.4 that caused excess throttling.

Worked example. Service with limit 2 CPUs, request 2, running 16 Tomcat/Netty worker threads. Quota per 100 ms: 200 ms. A spike of 16 busy threads burns 200 ms in 12.5 ms, then 87.5 ms frozen. Request latency p99 goes from 30 ms to 130 ms. Setting limit 4 (or removing it) and capping threads at 4 cut p99 back to 35 ms and nr_throttled to near zero.

Decision gravity. CPU limit: yes for noisy multi-tenant fairness, no for latency-critical services (use requests/weights). Memory limit: always. Both are reversible with a pod rollout.

Industry examples. Public writeups (Omio, Indeed, Zalando) blamed throttling for latency spikes and chose to drop CPU limits. Google Borg uses CPU shares plus per-class limits.

Everyday analogy. A prepaid data pack renewed every 100 ms: burn it all in the first 12 ms and the line is cut until renewal, even though the network is free.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading average CPU % and concluding no CPU problem.
  • Equating cpu: 1 with one core. It is 100 ms per 100 ms spread across any cores.
  • Not telling the runtime about the limit.

notes.title: Memory limits and OOM in containers
notes.html:
A memory limit (memory.max) is a hard ceiling for all processes in the cgroup: heap, stacks, page cache, kernel memory, tmpfs. When usage reaches the limit the kernel first tries to reclaim (drop clean page cache, swap if allowed); if it cannot, the cgroup OOM killer picks a process in that group and sends SIGKILL. No chance to log or clean up; the exit status is 137 (128 + 9) and Kubernetes shows OOMKilled.

$ kubectl describe pod api-7d9f | grep -A6 'Last State'
    Last State:   Terminated
      Reason:     OOMKilled
      Exit Code:  137
$ dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'
[Mon Nov  9 10:21:08] Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 18211 (java)
   total-vm:6291456kB, anon-rss:524288kB, file-rss:12288kB, shmem-rss:0kB
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.events
oom_kill 3
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.stat | head -6
anon 497000448       # heap, stack: cannot be dropped
file 12582912        # page cache: reclaimable
kernel 9437184

What counts toward the limit. Anonymous memory (heap), page cache from files the container touches (reclaimable, but under pressure it causes slow reclaim "thrashing" before OOM), tmpfs / emptyDir: medium: Memory, kernel structures. Hence "working set" (container_memory_working_set_bytes) = usage minus inactive file cache is what Kubernetes uses for eviction decisions.

Two different OOM kinds.

  • Container OOM (cgroup): the container hit its own limit; only it is killed.
  • Node OOM / eviction: the host is out of memory; the kubelet evicts pods (Evicted, per QoS class) or the global kernel OOM killer fires, scoring by oom_score_adj (Guaranteed pods get -997, BestEffort 1000).

Language runtime pitfalls.

  • JVM: heap is only part of memory (metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers, GC structures). -Xmx = limit means certain OOM kill. Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 (container aware since JDK 10; JDK 8u191+ backport). Example: limit 1 GiB, heap 700 MiB, rest 300 MiB for the other pieces.
  • Go: set GOMEMLIMIT to about 90% of the container limit (Go 1.19+) so the GC works harder before the kernel kills the process.
  • Node: --max-old-space-size below the limit.
  • Python / glibc malloc arenas: fragmentation raises RSS; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 often helps.
  • Memory leak vs just limit too low: a sawtooth that always returns to a baseline is fine; a ramp that never falls is a leak.

Worked example. A Java service has limit: 1Gi, -Xmx1g. Starting up it takes heap 600 MiB + metaspace 90 MiB + 200 threads x 1 MiB stacks + 150 MiB direct buffers = about 1.05 GiB. Under load the heap grows to 900 MiB and the pod dies with exit 137 every few hours; kubectl get pod shows restarts climbing. Fix: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65, limit 1.5Gi, and cap Netty direct memory with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m.

Swap. Kubernetes traditionally disabled swap on nodes; cgroup v2 memory.swap.max and the NodeSwap feature are now supported (check your version). With swap off, no cushion exists.

Decision gravity. Setting memory request = limit makes the pod Guaranteed-like for memory and predictable; overcommit (limit > request) risks node-level eviction. One-way for stateful data: a killed database can lose in-flight transactions, so size with headroom.

Industry examples. Common root causes in postmortems: JVM heap flags ignoring non-heap memory, tmpfs-backed emptyDir counting as memory, sidecar containers (Envoy) hitting small limits, and log buffers in memory.

Everyday analogy. A hotel room with a hard occupancy limit: the guests (heap), furniture (kernel structures) and luggage (page cache) all count; luggage can be moved out (reclaimed), but the guests are the problem.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit.
  • Confusing exit 137 with a crash in the app code. 137 is SIGKILL; check OOMKilled and dmesg.
  • Believing page cache does not count. It does, though it is reclaimable first.
  • Looking only at heap metrics while RSS includes much more.

notes.title: Debugging containers in production
notes.html:
You often have no shell, no tools, and a restarted pod that erased the evidence.

Workflow:

# 1. Why did it restart?
kubectl describe pod api-7d9f | grep -E 'Reason|Exit Code|Restart Count'
kubectl logs api-7d9f --previous              # logs of the crashed instance
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail

# 2. Live resource use from the container's own cgroup
kubectl exec api-7d9f -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat

# 3. Add tools without changing the image (ephemeral debug container sharing the target's namespaces)
kubectl debug -it api-7d9f --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api

# 4. From the node: enter just the network namespace and use host tools
PID=$(crictl inspect --output go-template --template '{{.info.pid}}' <container-id>)
nsenter -t $PID -n ss -tnp
nsenter -t $PID -n tcpdump -i eth0 -c 50 port 8080

Checklist for typical symptoms:

  • Restarts with 137: memory limit (see above).
  • Restarts with 143 or "Liveness probe failed": SIGTERM or probe timeout; a CPU-throttled app fails its probe; raise timeoutSeconds or the limit.
  • Latency spikes with low CPU%: nr_throttled in cpu.stat.
  • Pending pod: requests do not fit any node; kubectl describe shows Insufficient cpu.
  • Disk pressure / evictions: container logs and writable layers fill the node (ephemeral-storage limits).
  • DNS slow (5 s delays): conntrack races and ndots:5; use a node-local DNS cache.
  • Too many open files / pids.max reached: fork bomb or thread leak; check pids.current vs pids.max.

Industry examples. Netflix's Titus and Google's tooling capture cgroup stats continuously; cAdvisor (inside kubelet) exports container_* metrics that Prometheus scrapes.

Everyday analogy. Investigating a locked flat: first read the landlord's notes (orchestrator events), then the meters (cgroup), then ask the neighbours (host tools) before breaking in.

Common interview traps.

  • kubectl logs without --previous after a crash loop shows an empty new instance.
  • Judging resource problems from node-level graphs rather than per-container cgroup metrics.
  • Forgetting that exec into a distroless container fails; use an ephemeral container.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A container = Linux process + namespaces (see) + cgroups (use) + overlayfs root + capabilities/seccomp. It shares the host kernel; VMs do not.
  • Namespaces: PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP, TIME. Use nsenter and unshare to explore. Be careful with PID 1 and signals.
  • cgroups v2: memory.max, cpu.max, cpu.weight, pids.max; Kubernetes requests are scheduling hints and weights, limits are hard caps.
  • Docker stack: CLI, dockerd, containerd, runc; image layers via overlayfs with copy-up; keep data in volumes; run non-root with dropped capabilities.
  • CPU limit is a quota per 100 ms period: bursts of threads cause throttling and p99 spikes with low average CPU; watch nr_throttled; match runtime thread counts to the limit; consider requests-only for latency-critical services.
  • Memory limit is hard; OOM kill is SIGKILL, exit 137; JVM, Go, Node need limits below the container limit; page cache and tmpfs count.
  • Debug outside-in: kubectl describe/logs --previous, cgroup files, kubectl debug, nsenter.
